subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Might I ask whether the
committee discussed the matter of referring
Rules of the House

the estimates to a special committee? I remember that two years ago there was a motion introduced into the House asking that the estimates be referred to a select committee, and this resolution was referred to the special committee that was then engaged in revising the rules. I was wondering if this year's committee had discussed that matter at all.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Personally I am strongly in favour of the reference of the estimates of the various departments to a grand committee, composed of as many members as possible, before which all the experts, engineers, accountants, and other officials whose evidence might be required could be called and examined. When I was sitting on the other side of the House, in 1920 or 1921, I moved a resolution which was discussed for a whole afternoon by this House, and during the debate I referred to the fact that both in Great Britain and in the United States during the war a grand committee had been established for the purpose of sifting to the bottom all the expenditures involved by the participation of those two great countries in the war. It has been proven both in Great Britain and the United States that very large sums of money running up into millions and millions of dollars have been saved by the work of these committees. The committee in Great Britain reports to the House of Commons, which also resolves itself into committee of supply for the consideration of the estimates, but as every detail has previously been threshed out in the grand committee, and perhaps several items condemned, so to speak, the work of the committee of the whole House is very much shortened, in addition to the saving that is made by the careful scrutiny of proposed expenditures in the grand committee. But when I proposed to the committee revising the rules that they might adopt that principle, it was thought that perhaps it was too radical a change and that the House might not be ready to agree to it. I can assure the hon. member from Macleod that the proposal he makes will have my hearty support. Both in the United States and Great Britain during the war they had grand committees to which were referred all heavy expenditures, but it is true that those committees do not exist any more. I remember immediately after the war the United States official, General Dawes now vice-president, enumerated the vast sums of money they had saved to the American republic by that method. But it was thought that here it was too radical a step to take and that perhaps we might wait until

another opportunity presented itself before introducing that new system. If ever adopted we would have before that committee experts, accountants, engineers. Every detail would be explained and the report would be presented to the House. This committee would certainly be in earnest and non-partisan, and if the feeling was against a certain item that item would not be presented to the House.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
One point in connection
with the procedure before that committee is that under our present system all debates on ways and means and debates in committee of the whole are reported in Hansard. Under the proposed rules, and under the rules in the United States during the war, or the rule suggested by my hon. friend to my left, there would be no verbatim reports of the proceedings of that committee.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
During the war I
had some experience with the war appropriations. This question was discussed in the House of Commons, and it was decided that these sums would be voted under the title of war appropriations; detailed explanations of every item of the vote were printed and distributed to members of the House. The master was discussed in committee of the whole. I think the suggestion of the Speaker impracticable, because if you are going to submit to a special committee of the House every item of the estimates of every department I do not know when you will end the session.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think while the rules are
being revised- we should very carefully consider this matter. I think one of the reasons why we are revising the rules is to save time. Surely we could save a great deal of time if the estimates were referred to a committee. I would not suggest that we should have one committee only, but I think the estimates should be sent to four or five select committees of the House. At present we have a special committee to deal with the Canadian National estimates. I think nearly all hon. members will agree that is a great improvement over the old method of dealing with the estimates in committee of the whole House. If we send the estimates of the Canadian National railways to a special committee appointed to consider them, why not send the estimates of the Department of Agriculture to the committee on agriculture, and why not send all the other railway estimates to the special committee dealing with the Canadian National railway estimates? It would be very easy to divide all the other estimates among the different standing committees of

Rules oj the House
the House, allotting the estimates of each department to the committee dealing with that department. The reports of these committees would come before the House and be considered in committee of the whole House, and any hon. member who wanted to say something about them would have a chance. In that way I think we could shorten the session a month. Anybody who will read Hansard for the last four or five years will see that most of the time has been taken up with estimates. Hon. members wish to shorten the session, and I think we could achieve that object by adopting my suggestion more than in any other way. Before this committee which is revising the rules is disbanded, it should be asked to go into that matter and ascertain if we could not adopt that suggestion at the present time, and next session we could have the estimates referred to the select committee.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I entirely
support the suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod, and the suggestion of His Honour, the Speaker. I think there is nothing more aggravating or irritating, and nothing causes more delay than the practice of having ministers come into the chamber with a deputy in front of them, endeavouring to make explanations of subjects on which they are not informed and cannot be informed. I am not blaming the ministers. I understand their difficulties. Having to meet every day in council, they have not time to study the estimates or become acquainted with the details in connection with them. They have before them a very brief description of the particular matter that may be under consideration at the moment, and) as to the reason it is necessary, but when we come to the engineering end of it, or the justifiability of it, we have not the information and cannot obtain it because of the method of handling the estimates. It is the most stupid and foolish method of spending the public money, and I think my hon. friend's suggestion one that we might wisely adopt.
I submit that the point brought forward by my hon. friend from Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) was not well taken, because I did not understand the suggestion made by the hon. the Speaker, nor the suggestion made by the hon. member for Mhcleod to be that there should be a printed explanation of the estimates in detail handed to every hon. member. I entirely agree that such a proposition would [DOT]be impracticable and ridiculous. It would involve volumes of printing, but the other suggestion is a practical one. Let us refer the estimates to the several committees, as
we are doing in the case of the Canadian National, or refer them to a special standing committee as suggested by the hon. member for Macleod. It would be a great improvement, and we could go back feeling satisfied with the manner in which we had dealt with this question. I think nobody can go home now feeling that this matter has been dealt with satisfactorily.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think I will have to
come to the rescue of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: We are not interested any more than other members.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friends are running the government. I do not see how any self-respecting minister can recommend to this House estimates, previously recommended by the cabinet, and then have them tom to pieces by special committees. The thing is absolutely absurd. I would not remain on the government benches five minutes if some committee of the House, having no responsibility at all, could tell me what I could do or what I could not do. We must have some respect for the minister and he must have some responsibility. It is aibsurd to tell a minister after he has brought down his estimates, and after they have been submitted to the committee, that he cannot spend this money. I do not think you could get any self-respecting government to permit themselves to be placed in that position.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think we are discussing this case from the viewpoint of the ministers. I have no doubt that they know all about their departments and what the estimates are for; but we do not. I have observed that the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. MicGibbon) and his associates ask a great many questions in supply-many of them perhaps are not of much consequence. While the estimates are under consideration a good deal of political campaigning takes place, and we ask questions which perhaps should not be answered at all. The time of the House is wasted more in that respect than in connection with any other business. Surely we should now refer this question back to the special committee while we deal with the rest of the rules, so that they may draft a rule that will enable us to handle the estimates more efficiently and save the time of the House. The suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Ooote) would certainly have this effect, for if members want information on any items they could secure it before the various committees to which those items had been referred. If we were to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for

Rules of the House

Muskoka there would be no use in bringing the estimates before the House at all. It is suggested that we let the cabinet deal with the estimates; but if there is to be any inquiry as to the particular items, that inquiry should take place in a small committee. I therefore suggest that His Honour the Speaker place this rule before the committee for amendment.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Don't be in such a hurry
to carry things until we know what we are actually carrying.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I say to my hon.
friend that this would involve more than a mere change in procedure? It would affect the principle of the discussion of the estimates in the House when every member is present to scrutinize the expenditure of public money. speechtext:
It simply

speechtext:
I will plead my hon.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Everyone understood, I

I do not think
a proposal of this kind would shorten sessions. Imagine, if you can, all the estimates going to the different committees, with your experts in attendance. I notice this rule as amended is substantially different from the same rule as amended last year. The object of this amended rule is to do away with the practice of members loading up the order paper with resolutions during the recess. Then when we
come down here we find perhaps thirty or forty resolutions which have been placed on the order paper during the recess; I think in one case I counted as many as fifteen resolutions in the name of one private member. The object of the farmer committee was to try and get away from that; that object was attained in some measure, but subsection 4 of the proposed amendment of last year has been left out. That subsection provided that if notice of certain resolutions were given during the recess, these should not be placed on the order paper in the order in which they were received but that they should be retained by the clerk and on the opening day of the session the right of precedence should be determined by ballot. According to this new rule, a member may only have one resolution on the order paper at one time, and it is suggested that this will do away with this abuse. That will not be the case, because a member may put down a resolution in his own name and then put the other fourteen resolutions in the names of his friends in the House, which will load up the order paper just the same. We are always in the habit of running to the English parliament for precedents, and I might say that in that House 'the ballot system is followed. I do not know why that was left out of the amended rule, because it seems to me it would cover the whole situation.

I will not waste time in forcing another vote, but I want to go on record once more as entirely opposed to the changes made by which the speeches of private members will be limited to forty minutes on all occasions. One hon. member opposite said that the British House of Commons was originally instituted to vote supply. Yes, but there was a condjition attached to it. Before they voted supplies they made the king listen to the grievances of the common people, and it is the inalienable right of the common people to present their grievances in the House of Commons, but the House has dealt a blow against that principle to-day. While the amendment was carried a little while ago I think that the greater tribunal, the people of Canada will justify us who opposed it in the position we took. I think the most precious political rights the British subject can possess are, first of all, the right to vote, and second, the right of untrammelled free speech, and I believe the House has struck a blow at that right to-day.

I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to provide anything this year for accommodation at Georgetown or Souris. The question of accommodation at Georgetown has been before the government for a couple of years at least, and it was generally expected that something would certainly be done this year. I brought it up in the House last session, and the then Minister of Public Works stated that the government, having considered the matter, intended to proceed, but that owing to the railway east of Charlottetown being narrow gauge, it was no use constructing a warehouse until the gauge was standardized. This was done last September, and the people of the province have been hoping that this very much needed accommodation would be provided, It is not a local matter affecting merely George-

town or even Kings county, it is a matter for the province as a whole. For at least a month after the harbours of Charlottetown and Summerside are closed in December Georgetown and Souris are open. The growing of seed potatoes is now a very important industry in Prince Edward Island, and their transportation has become an acute problem. As is well known, the car ferry during the past year was taxed to its utmost capacity, and was unable to transport all the produce grown in the province. Although it worked day and night during November last it was unable to carry all the traffic offered. There will be great disappointment if something is not done this year to provide the necessary accommodation, by reason of the fact that a large portion of the seed potatoes is sold in the southern part of the United States, and it is very important that this traffic should be moved by water. In certain parts of the south they will purchase these seed potatoes only about the middle of January when their planting season commences. Transportation by rail is very expensive; it is also risky on account of frost at that time of year, and they will not ship till late in the season because they have no storage facilities there and do not want to hold potatoes for a month or six weeks. Therefore they want transportation by water at the latest possible date. Last year the latest date on which navigation was open at Charlottetown and Summerside was during the first few days of December, while a steamer loaded a cargo of produce in the harbour of Georgetown on January 11. Navigation could have been continued for many days later had any business been offered or had there been accommodation.

I might ask my friend
a question which he can answer in the course of his remarks. I have received representations with regard to both Souris and Georgetown, and as to the relative amounts of potatoes shipped from both places. There is no doubt that there is quite an extensive traffic in potatoes, which I understand to be largely seed potatoes shipped to the United States from both these places. Would my friend feel disposed, in case the government should not feel able to grant both requests, to state which is the larger? The figures differ somewhat.

I would say to the minister that the local traffic is not considered in the matter as of any consequence, although of course it is important to the people of these different localities. I am not speaking for the county of Kings or for

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
the towns of Georgetown or Souris; I am speaking for the province of Prince Edward Island. Queens county is just as much interested as Kings county, because the main features apply equally to both. The harbour of Souris cannot be used as a shipping point during the month of December because it has no storage facilities, and the people in the vicinity of Georgetown cannot use that point either; if either Georgetown or Souris were equipped with the necessary accommodation the whole province would be able to make use of that accommodation. The farmers would then be able to get their produce to the southern states at the time the consumers want it, and the farmers would realize a great deal more than would otherwise be the case. I was proceeding to give the reasons for that statement. If the potatoes are transported by water they can be delivered in the southern United States at a price which will cover both freight and duty if shipped by rail, and when you realize that the duty is thirty cents per hundred pounds and that you can save at least that amount if not more by water transportation, it will be seen that this is a very important item.
I would not like to say to the minister that he should select one point or the other, because either port will serve the great bulk of the province. I think the government officials and engineers should decide on the point where this warehouse should be placed. A meeting of the potato growers was held at Souris about two weeks ago, at which strong representations were made from the local standpoint that this warehouse should be placed at Souris, while I understand that up ' to that time all negotiations by the department were made with the view to having this warehouse at Georgetown. I understand the department has prepared plans for that warehouse, and it was generally accepted in the province that these facilities would be constructed at that point. Beyond that I have not anything to say in the matter; it is entirely up to the government and its officials to decide the proper point at which to place this warehouse. As a matter of fact, if we had nerve enough to ask for it, accommodation should be placed at both these points, but we realize that we must be reasonable and must be satisfied if the Department of Public Works will grant us one warehouse at this time.
There are many reasons which could be given for accommodation at these points other than the local needs of these places. There are a number of places in the eastern and northern parts of the province which have no
railway accommodation whatever but have water accommodation, such as Murray Harbour North, Lower Montague, Gaspereaux, Newport, Bridgetown, Fortune and some points on the north side as far around as New London in Queen's county. These and other points would be served by accommodation at either Souris or Georgetown, because these people would be able at any season of the year to assemble their produce at Georgetown or Souris by means of small schooners, large motor boats or other means of water transportation, without fear of frost. This is a most important matter; while I do not like to take up too much time of the House I would iike to go further into it, but I hardly think it necessary. I think probably the minister has all the information required, and if there is anything further he would like to ask I would be gladl to tell him.
Before closing I would like to say that when this matter was brought up last year the minister practically told us the warehouse would be built after the railway was standardized. The Prime Minister was at Georgetown last year; at that time this matter was put up to him very strongly, and the people at the meeting understood his statement to be a practical promise that a warehouse would be built at Georgetown. I think I am justified in saying that-and I am not speaking politically at all but rather in the interests of the industry in Prince Edward Island because The Patriot newspaper, which is the Liberal prgan in that province, reported Mr. Mackenzie King as follows:
Mr. King spoke of his landing at Georgetown and of the discussion in parliament as to the need of improved facilities at that port.
He was interested in seeing the large warehouse on the railway wharf which had been referred to. He did not wish to be charged with making promises to influence the electors, but as a result of representations made to him, the Liberal government had taken steps to have this shed made frost-proof. The then Minister of Public Works, Hon. Dr. King, had declared that as soon as the standardization of the railway east was completed the work of making the warehouse frost-proof would be undertaken.
"I believe that this would be a right and proper step, and should be undertaken as soon as possible," declared Hon. Mr. King, amid loud applause.
The people of that section of the country took that statement as a definite promise, in conjunction with the statement made by the then Minister of Public Works, that this work would be proceeded with without delay and that the accommodation which is so milch needed would be granted. There is great disappointment in that province to-day because of the fact that no sum has been placed in

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
the estimates this year to provide for this work.
It must also be remembered that even during the open season, the harbour of Charlottetown was taxed last year to its utmost capacity, and as a result about 800,000 bushels of potatoes were shipped from that port. About 200,000 bushels passed through the port of Summerside, and an additional 200,000 bushels were handled by schooners and other sailing craft. The car ferry, during the shipping months, handled 2,271 carloads; as I said before, during the month of November the car ferry worked day and night and was taxed to its utmost capacity, handling about 1,165 car loads. These figures are taken from the records of the railway officials. I am satisfied that about the utmost that could be handled, with the rail and water facilities available, was handled last fall. Unless some further accommodation is given so that larger shipments can be made, there is a prospect that we shall be seriously handicapped in the matter of shipping facilities next fall.

I may say to my hon. friend that representations have been made by at least two delegations on behalf of Georgetown, and one or more on behalf of Souris. They have pointed out that the potato industry in Prince Edward island has doubled in production in the last three or four years, and the exports have more than trebled. There is a great difference of opinion [DOT] between the representatives of these two places as to. which port is best entitled to consideration. I do not think that either of them quite" expected that much could be done for both. However, a survey of the Souris district is now being made, and I shall be very glad to go into the matter further as soon as that report is received.

I should like to say for the information of the House that potato growing in Prince Edward island is going ahead at a very rapid rate. The votes included in the estimates we are considering were inserted there for the purpose of making provision for the expansion of this particular industry. In order to show hon. gentlemen just how important the matter is, I shall quote from the issue, dated February 19, last, of the Commercial Intelligence Journal, gotten out by the Department of Trade and Commerce, wherein appears an article by Trade Commissioner Frederick Hudd on Canada's trade with the United States. In the course of this article the Commissioner says:
Undoubtedly a considerable portion of the total exports of potatoes from Canada to the

United States were reexported to other markets, although detailed statistics on this point are not available. It is evident, however, that the reputation of the Canadian potato, as well as its superior quality and size, are finding for it a constantly expanding market, not only in the United States but in foreign countries through United States agencies. Improved methods of cleaning, grading, and packing Canadian potatoes have greatly assisted their marketing in competition with potatoes from the New England states. Under present conditions the heavy movement of potatoes from maritime province points in the months of November and April results in a congestion necessitating the placing of an embargo on potato shipments at such points as Boston and New York. This congestion at two periods results in a lower price for the producer. After having obtained a first hand knowledge of the potato situation, par-icularly in Prince Edward island, the writer is of the opinion that it would be of considerable advantage if there were more frost proof warehouse facilities on railway tracks at Canadian shipping points. Potatoes could then be stored and shipments spread over a period, thereby eliminating the risk of loss due to lack of frost proof storage for potatoes 'which it is impossible to ship when the movement is at peak.
There was included in the estimates of last year the sum of $75,000 for the desired work at Charlottetown, but it was not available in time. The railway authorities therefore, agreed that they would underbake the work with the understanding that they would be reimbursed later on by the Public Works department. To show you what effect this work has had in connection with the industry I beg to put on Hansard a letter written to me on December 7, 1926 by the secretary of the Prince Ediward Island Potato Growers' Association. That letter is as follows:
Dear Mr. Jenkins:
I feel that as an association we should express to you our appreciation of your efforts in securing for us at Charlottetown a better warehouse for the handling of our potatoes.
This season we had in storage during cold weather potatoes in value from seventy-five to one hundred thousand dollars. This was due to the late arrival of steamers over which we have no control, and you can readily understand how great would have been our loss in the old shed. While that is the most important advantage, yet loading as we did such large cargoes we could never have been able to accomplish the moving of upwards of seven hundred thousand bushels in practically six weeks with the old facilities.
We wish to assure you the expenditure has been a benefit to the whole province, and we feel you were of great assistance in bringing the government to see the need for the changes made.
Yours very truly,
J. W. Boultek,
Secretary,
P.E.I. Potato Growers Association.
I may say, Sir, that I happened to be a member of the House last year and we were

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
very ably assisted not only by the members from Prince Edward Island, but also by the Hon. John Sinclair, although not at that time a member of the House, who helped us in every way possible.
I am very much pleased to support the recommendations made by the member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald). It is quite true, as he has stated, that the harbours of Souris and Georgetown remain open quite a while longer than either those of Charlottetown or Summerside, and it is therefore essential that we should have later shipments from ports such as these. I shall be pleased to support anything that will give us better shipping facilities for the island at large. As the member for Kings has stated, it is really a provincial and not a county matter. There seems to be, unfortunately, a little difficulty as to what port should be selected for improvement. I would suggest, however, just as he has suggested, that a representative of the department should be sent down to the island to go over the different ports and recommend to the department the proper steps which ought to be taken. I shall be pleased indeed to support whatever recommendation is made by the officer sent down for that purpose. The wonderful work going on in the province is really marvelous to those who are not acquainted with the situation, and any assistance that will help to place the products of Prince Edward island on the outside markets in good condition is something which merits the utmost consideration of the government.

I will delay
the committee only a few moments in a brief expression of opinion with respect to the very important matter now under consideration. I want to say that I agree with the representations that have been made by the member for Kings, and by the member for Queens (Mr. Jenkins) in regard to the necessity of making further provision to aid in the transportation of potatoes from Prince Edward island at a later period in the season. Perhaps, Sir, the two main reasons may be summed up in this way: at present our season for shipping potatoes, after the close of the harvesting period, is forty days. Now, if we can extend that by a month we shall be conferring a great benefit upon the growers of potatoes in the province. Further than that we shall enjoy the advantage of a much larger market in the southern states by shipping potatoes to those people when they require them, which is in the month of January. We can do that if facilities are provided in the eastern or winter ports. With that end in view I say to the minister that
it is necessary that one harbour at least in the eastern end of Prince Edward Island be equipped for winter shipments so as to take care of exportations of seed potatoes to the southern states at the season of the year when such shipments are most advantageous.
I may say further that I agree with the minister that if representations have been made to have developments carried out at two ports he could not do otherwise than have a proper survey undertaken and act on the advice of his representative on the ground.
I think further, as an agriculturist representing an agricultural constituency, that it would be wise for the Minister of Agriculture to have an expert from his department look into the situation also with a view to having the best possible transportation facilities provided for the exportation of potatoes, particularly from the point of view of making shipments in the winter season possible by water.

I am not
quite clear as to the minister's explanation; in fact he has not given any explanation as to why a sum of money was not put in the estimates this year for this purpose. It has been before the government, it has been in the hands of the Department of Public Works for at least two or three years. Last year, according to Hansard, the answer I received from the then Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay), was as follows:
I am familiar with the situation at Georgetown. The government have reconditioned and renewed a very good wharf at that point, and have improved the shed accommodation. It is true that we have not made that shed frost proof, as I think it should be, for the accommodation of the farmers in the handling of their potatoes, but I would point out that at the present time the railway is on the narrow gauge. We understand that the railway is changing to the broad gauge, and once that is accomplished I think we will be justified in spending some money on a potato warehouse at Georgetown.
I do not want to be critical at all but, in view of the facts as set out, in view of the promise virtually given by the minister in the House last year, and the Prime Minister's virtual promise at Georgetown, I do not quite understand why something was not included in the estimates this year for either one of these ports. The minister will agree with me, I think, that it is only within the last few weeks, since the estimates were prepared and printed, that any representations were made to him with regard to Souris. I understand that the first step taken was a meeting held at Souris about two weeks ago, not over three weeks at any rate, and after that a delegation came to interview the minister, resolutions having been forwarded to

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
him as adopted at that meeting. Surely the department having had the matter under consideration for at least two years, would have been prepared, if they intended doing so, to put an item in the estimates this year to implement the promises made by the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister. I should like to have the minister's candid explanation as to why this was not done in view of these promises, or at any rate of what we regard in that light.

The representations on
behalf of Georgetown, made shortly prior to the preparation of the estimates, asked, as I recollect, for a frost proof potato warehouse much larger than called for in the first estimate, and it was necessary to have a resurvey made before any decision could be arrived at. The warehouse which had been discussed before was stated by the representatives from Georgetown to be totally inadequate to the present needs of that port, and consequently a further survey was made. That survey was not completed nor reported upon when the estimates were in preparation, and in the meantime Souris represented that the production there was four times as large as the production at Georgetown. That matter is now being inquired into.

It is not at all a question of production at either Souris or Georgetown ; that is only a minor detail in connection with the scheme. Does the minister intend to put anything in the supplementary estimates this year for this work at either of these places?

That will depend; upon
t'he reports received. I am not in a position to answer that question.

Am I to
assume that it is not the intention of the government to do anything this year in regard to this matter?
My hon. friend should not assume that. I want him to understand clearly that I cannot give an undertaking to include any amount in the estimates for either Souris or Georgetown or any other place.

Item agreed to.
Summerside-wharf repairs and improve-mets, $63,000.
_ Mr. MACDONALD (Kings):	The minister might explain what this vote is intended for. What construction is contemplated?

The proposed work will
consist of:
(1)	Rebuilding outer end and outer west side of wharf to original width of 100 feet on a length of 350 feet.
(2)	Construction of two warehouses each 230 feet long, 26 feet wide.
(3)	Provision for two lines of railway track between the sheds above referred to.

I was not
objecting; I just wanted the information.

Item agreed to.
West Point-wharf repairs, $6,800.

Before this
resolution is reported I have just one remark to make. We have in this total vote $189,600 for the province of Prince Edward Island, and it will be found on analysis that almost every dollar of that money, with the exception of a small item for Naufrage, is to be spent in Queens and Prince counties. There is just $1,000 for Kings county. The department is fully aware, from information submitted by its district engineer, how urgent the needs of Kings county are, and it is surprising to find that of this large sum of money practically every cent is to go to Queens and Prince counties and only $1,000 to Kings county. Naturally I feel, as the people of Kings county feel, that we should not be shut out altogether even though by a small majority they voted me here instead of returning a supporter of the government.

My hon. friend is overlooking the fact that these items are made up largely of work in Charlottetown amounting to $75,000 and the vote for Summerside of $63,000, which are the recommendations of the Duncan report.

But apart
from that there is $50,000 for the other counties and1 nothing for Kings.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and Rivers

New Brunswick, $154.100.

On looking over this
list of places provided for in New Brunswick I fail to see the name of Lomeville. It has been brought to the attention of the department on several occasions by my colleague and myself. Lomeville is an important and thriving fishing village. The catch of fish is quite considerable and valuable, including a large catch of salmon. In the harbour of Lomeville there is a pier which is more useful as a breakwater than for the ordinary purposes of a wharf. Last year the department

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
made some repairs to this structure, but it did not and does not meet the great requirement of the pier as a breakwater. The water is shallow in the harbour and the fishermen are not able to use the pier as a breakwater in rough weather. There is therefore need of some dredging; not a great deal is required but a fair amount will have to be done. If the minister would look into the matter he would be satisfied that some dredging at that point would be a very justifiable expenditure. It would enable the fishermen to bring their boats in for safety in rough weather. I do not know whether the minister has considered this matter or had it brought to his attention; perhaps not; I think he only came into office since last year. But I would ask him, and I have no doubt my colleague will do the same thing, that some work be done at this point. It is an important centre, a thriving, active port composed of fishermen making a valuable catch of fish of all kinds, and it is about twenty miles from St. John. These fishermen cannot carry on with safety because there is no shelter in time of storm.

I shall be glad to consider the representations my hon. friend has made.
I am advised that certain repairs were made last year at this place, but they were of a temporary character, I believe, and did not extend to the dredging. However, the matter will be looked into, and if it is not very extensive there is a possibility that it might be taken care of under the general vote for harbours and rivers.
What amount was spent in this province last year in comparison with the amount asked for?

My hon. friend will realize that last year was an unusual year, because we were allowed to proceed only with matters that could be gone ahead with under governor general's warrants. The total expenditure last year was around $200,400. The total asked for this year is $154,100.
Last year's estimate was $292,925.
Yes, and $92,525 of that amount was not expended.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and Rivers-Quebec-Cap de la Madeleine-wharf extension, $75,000.
Would the minister explain this vote?

The proposed work consists of a close face cribwork extension to the downstream end of the headblock, 200 feet
long by 90 feet wide; stone filled cribwork to be around the outside, and the centre filled with earth and stone, and the whole covered with a bituminous macadam flooring.
Is this the total estimate for the completion of the work?
No. The total estimated cost was $132,800. We have received tenders varying from $110,000 to $174,000.
Are the tenders let?
No contract has been let yet.

Item agreed to.
St-Louis river-dredging, $46,200.
Would the minister explain this item?

The proposed work estimated at $46,200 is towards dredging a section of the St. Louis river, 3.35 miles long to a depth of 6i feet and a width of 40 feet, to complete the scheme of improvements commenced in 1905 and running over a period of years up to 1916. This work wild be done by an excavator on caterpillar wheels which will have to be purchased or built, as well as a scow 25 feet by 40 feet.
Is this to complete the work?

It will complete the work in that particular section, but this is only part of the general scheme.
Item agreed. to.
Sorel-harbour improvements, $46,100.
What is the explanation of this item?

The details are as follows:
(1)	Reconstruction in concrete of remaining 311.4 feet of high level
wharf along the Richelieu river.. $18,000
(2)	Repairs to breakwater	 2,000
(3)	Reconstruction, Pontbriand wharf, the new structure to consist of a closeface crib structure built on piles,
250 feet long and 14 feet wide, with a 27 feet return wing at each end and concrete anchor blocks 4 feet by 4 feet by 5 feet placed at every
25 feet	 23,000
(4)	To build a reinforced concrete roadway 511 feet long by 20 feet wide connecting the end of Roy street to the high level wharf; and a concrete sidewalk 4 feet wide by approximately 390 feet long around the end
of	the high level wharf	 6,100
Total	$49,100
Less	work authorized 1926-1927.. ..	3,000
Balance for 1927-1928	$46,100
Item agreed to.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Valleyfield-dredging, $50,000.
Last year we passed an item of $31,000 for dredging at this point. Was all that money expended, and will the amount asked for here complete this dredging project?
No. The $31,000 appears as a revote, and we are asking for an additional $19,000 to complete the work.

Item agreed to.	.
Harbours and rivers-Ontario, $1,021,150.

I would like to ask the
minister whether there is under contemplation any expenditure in supplementaries for the harbour at the city of Oshawa.
Representations have been made by various representatives from that district, including my hon. friend, if I remember correctly, and the matter is under consideration.

I am very glad to hear the minister is contemplating taking action, but in fairness to the district I represent I would like to make a statement. It surely must appear to everyone that there is something absurd in the harbour situation at Okhawa. Here we have a city which contributes a larger revenue to this government than any other place in the Dominion with the exception of five. Only five ports in Canadh. send more revenue to Ottawa than the city of Oshawa. It must strike hon. members as a marvelous thing that a city of our size should send to Ottawa $30,000 every day from customs receipts. We have never asked very much from the Dominion of Canada; we have not made many requests, but twenty-six years ago a Liberal government undertook to build a harbour at Oshawa. By virtue. of that promise what harbour we had was destroyed1, and after twenty-six years the condition remains the same. There is no politics in this matter; both Liberal and Conservative governments decided years ago that we should have our harbour works completed in that town. The last few years the government voted reasonable supplies and carried on some work which up to to-day has cost $132,000. It will take $112,000 to finish the work. I have recently inspected the works and have taken friends to see it during wintertime, and I say that unless the government completes the work, all that has already been done will be destroyed. It is a necessary work. Our city needs it. There are at the present time men who are quite ready to build coal sheds and do other Work which will assist us in our progress and in our undertakings. The harbour is more than half completed1, but it has taken twenty-

six years to get to this stage. Surely we are not doing anything out of the way in presenting our case to parliament. All we ask is that the work that has been undertaken be finished. It is a small demand in comparison to what we contribute to the revenue of the country. I am glad to hear that the government has the matter under consideration and I hope they will complete it. It will be a benefit to the town, and will more than pay the government of Canada if they complete it. Men in Oshawa have 'built stores and warehouses at Montreal and are prepared1 to ship their goods, but they ,have been standing there several years waiting for the harbour to be completed. I plead with the government to consider this matter and put something in the supplementary estimates of a substantial nature to finish the work which has been dragging along for twenty-six years.

I do not expect the minister to carry everything in his head, but in the supplementary estimates last year there was a vote of, I think, $5,000 for repairs for navigation purposes at what we call the Narrows in Muskoka lakes. It does not appear in the main estimates this year; will it appear in the supplementaries?

Nobody knows what will
be in the supplementaries until council considers them. Sometimes the minister is disappointed when he asks for certain estimates, but this matter will receive consideration.
Will the minister give " favourable consideration," as Sir Oliver Mowat used to say?
It will receive grave consideration.

I have been looking
through the estimates for Ontario and I could not realize what was the matter. There seemed to be something missing. What is the matter with Belle river now? Is that completed, or why is it there is no amount in the estimates for Belle river?

There is very extensive
work at Belle river. It has been completed as far as the government intend to go at the present time.

Does it complete one
pier on one side and one pier on the other side?
One pier on one side.

Does it accomplish
anything for the purpose required?

Oh, yes. This government never does anything that does not accomplish something.

Georgian Bay Canal Company

With regard to the
grant for a wharf at Ottawa, is it a new project, and where is it?

That is to take the place
of the wharf at the basin on the Rideau canal.

Where is it-on the
Rideau?

No, it is on the canal.
Conferences are taking place with the railway department and negotiations are under way to decide upon the exact location.

Is there any use for a
wharf at that point on the canal?

My information is that
on the canal basin they do $7,000,000 worth of business a year, and it is very necessary. We are taking the present structure away, and some substitute must be provided for it.

There is only one other vote in this item that I want information about, and that is with regard to the dredging at Toronto. I understood the waterfront was under the harbour commission. Is that under the harbour commission or outside of the commission?

This is not the waterfront; it is the eastern end, and there has to be additional dredging there every year; there seems to be an annual filling in.
Item agreet" to.
Harbours ant* livers-Manitoba-$22,400.

Last year in the
supplementaries an item was included for the purpose of providing against flood conditions in the southern part of Manitoba because of certain works -that had been constructed to the south of the line. Is that project to be undertaken?

I believe my hon. friend
is referring to the Roseau river, which is an international stream. I think the control of the water has been referred to the International Joint Commission. The matter is receiving consideration and if we decide to proceed the necessary vote will appear in the supplementaries.

Item agreed to.
Saskatchewan and Alberta-Fort Resolution -wharf, $18,000.
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $10,000.

Whereabouts are the
harbours in Alberta?
They are in the northern part of Alberta, being the points along the river where there is water transportation.
The vote has nothing to do with measuring the current of the river?
No.

How much was spent
under this vote last year?
Out of the $15,000?
Out of the $10,000.

Is not Fort
Resolution in the Northwest Territories? I think it should be separated from this vote.
Yes, it is in the Mackenzie district.

Item agreed to.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably 1 would not have taken up very much time in respect to this matter had it not been for the rather uncalled-for attacks which were made yesterday by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) and the general terms of insinuation which characterized the major part of his observations. For the benefit of this House I desire to state at once that while I think the personal business of members of parliament should be sacred from the prying eyes of the public, nevertheless when they are dragged into the House of Commons it becomes essential that some observations should be -made by those who are directly affected.



Georgian Bay Canal Company
For a period of upwards of fifteen years I have been associated with the enterprise known as The E. B. Eddy Company, Limited, which company many years ago purchased a limit on the Gatineau river together with the late Senator Edwards; subsequently, after his interest had been sold, the company acquired the whole limit. The other license holder on the river is the Canadian International Paper Company, and in consequence of the develop. ment they are carrying on I found it necessary to speak to the president of that enterprise as to what the effect of their operations might be upon the business of the company with which I was associated. He at once assured me that he had no desire prejudicially to affect those interests, and later suggested that I might join the board of his company. This I did, in common with many others, one at least being the leader of the government in the Senate, and thus I found myself for the first time associated with such a considerable number of distinguished Liberals. You can readily understand what a splendid effect this association has had upon me, and how much it has induced me to believe that the liberality of their views is not confined1 to their politics.
Might I venture further, and assert that I think no very good purpose was served in this House by the attacks made by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) upon the good faith, the honesty and integrity of either newspapers, newspaper men or men of business carrying on their operations in this Ottawa valley. One hearing that speech or reading it afterwards could not but be struck with the rather violent attacks made against the president, for instance, of the Canadian International Paper Company. There is no young man of my acquaintance in the United States, Mr. Speaker, who has made his way by perseverance, by very great ability and the exercise of his great talents as has Mr. Graustein. He has been honoured in the country in which he lives, and his enterprises have received the slamp of approval of Hon. Mr. Taschereau, Premier of Quebec. Therefore I think it ill becomes any Liberal member of this House of Commons thus to attack him where he has no opportunity to make his defence. So far as his business operations are concerned, they have all been carried out under the law. If one for a moment remembers that after all the observations made by the hon. gentleman have nothing whatever to do with the bill under discussion, one finds it even more difficult to explain them, but when one recalls the genial qualities of heart and mind which characterize the hon. member for Ottawa, one is after all inclined to excuse and forgive him
IMr. Bennett.]
and to remember that the principals whom he represents are capable of nothing better.

Assume it does-and here is where some of my friends opposite have, I submit with deference, fallen into a very grave error with respect to sending a bill to committee-I am going to venture even although it may be tiresome, to read some of the authorities dealing with a measure of this

kind. That brings me at once to what I conceive to be the essential feature to keep in mind with respect to this matter. It is usual with respect to private bills to give them their second reading as a matter of form. That is usual; I desire to make that perfectly clear, and usually there are very few speeches made with respect to the second reading, unless there be some matter of public interest involved which overshadows the private right. Indeed, it is the almost universal custom for the bill to go to committee. The authorities make that abundantly clear. Let us for a moment look at what the authorities say. At pages 709 and 710 of May the position is stated in these words- I shall not read too many authorities, but I desire to make this point perfectly clear:
The second reading of a private bill corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the House affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons: but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the House will not consent to the second reading: but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
Now I desire to say once more that this House in accepting the principle of a private bill on its second reading may be said usually only to do so conditionally, because the proceedings with respect to a private bill are partly legislative and partly judicial; before the House, they are legislative; before the committee, they are judicial. It becomes necessary and essential for the promoters of the bill to prove their facts before the committee; otherwise, they fail to get their legislation. But it must be observed further that where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the House will not consent to the second reading.
Now my contention to this House, Sir, is that this is a bill where, irrespective of the facts, the principle is objectionable.

He has kept clearly before him the distinction between a private bill and a public measure, and in that he is supported by the authorities in England. I desire to point out the principle upon which they proceed. I cite only a few authorities. I will point out to you that in England this bill could not possibly receive consideration or attention as a private bill, and I am going to show you the authorities, if I may, Sir, because I conceive it to be somewhat important that we should in this parliament recognize that a bill which at its inception thirty years ago may have been purely a private bill, may by reason cf changed conditions, by the alterations of the law, by the development of the country, by industrial demands, by all the conditions that go to make a progressing civilization, become a public measure, and thereby lose its status as a private bill. Let me point out what is said in May. Commenting at page 657 upon private and public bills, he says:
Bills for the particular interest or benefit of any person or persons, are treated, in parliament, as private bills. Whether they be for the interest of an individual, of a public company or corporation, or of a parish, city, county, or other locality, they are equally distinguished from measures of public policy; and this _decision is marked in the very manner of their introduction. Every private bill is solicited by the parties themselves wlio are interested in promoting it, being founded upon a imtition which must be duly deposited in accordance with standing order.
Then, after reviewing a number of cases, the learned author proceeds to indicate the real difficulties that are encountered when you come to a bill of this character. He says:
In passing private bills, parliament still exercises its legislative functions, but its proceedings partake also of a judicial character. The persons whose private interests are to be promoted appear as suitors for the bill; while those who apprehend injury are admitted as adverse parties in the suit. Many of the formalities of a court of justice are maintained; various conditions are required to be observed, and their observance to be strictly proved; and if the parties do not sustain the bill in its progress, by following every regulation and form prescribed, it is not forwarded by the House in which it is pending. If they abandon it, and no other parties undertake its support the bill is lost, however sensible the House may be of its value.
He proceeds further to point out that in England a number of bills that were introduced as private bills had to be withdrawn. Then at page 667 there is a review of a number of cases. He says, for instance:
In 1900, on the second reading of a private bill promoted by the Metropolitan Water Companies, the Speaker called the attention of the House to the large and important powers which were propoed to be conferred by it upon a pubic department (the Local Government Board), and which, according to the practice of the House, ought to be secured by a public rather than by a private bill; and the bill was accordingly withdrawn.
In 1910, on the second reading of the Society of Apothecaries of London Bill which had been introduced as a private bill, the Speaker drew attention to the fact that the bill sought to empower the society to grant diplomas in sanitary science and public health, and for dentistry and dental surgery, and ruled that it should proceed as a public bill, as it dealt with public interests; and the bill was accordingly withdrawn.
And the same with another bill, and still another. I need not go into details. All the authorities go to show that where it appears from the statement of the powers sought or the principle which the House is asked to support that any measure affects public interests of large and wide character, it ceases to be a private bill and must be dealt with as a public measure. That is the summary of the position. It is for that reason that the leader of the opposition has moved, not that this bill should be given the six months' hoist or read three months hence, but an amendment declaring that a bill which confers upon a private corporation powers so large, over two hundred miles of river and lake waters, is a public bill, not a private bill, and cannot be dealt with by the House as a private measure.

Mr. Chairman, I would like

of the Minister of Public Works to some grave omissions with regard to the constituency of Skeena which I trust will be included in the supplementary estimates of this year. I have already brought some of these things to the notice of the minister and there are others to follow, but I would now ask that the minister give his careful consideration to some very pressing needs of that constituency. Port Simpson, which lies near Prince Rupert, is a federal port, and possesses a wharf which at this moment is in a serious state of disrepair; its state is precarious, and the residents of that town have urged me to present their case to the government for immediate consideration. I can say without exaggeration that there is a moral obligation on the government to safeguard the lives of the people who are using that wharf; the whole structure is decayed; there is danger of its collapse, and as it is used by all the incoming vessels, the Union boats as well as the large fishing boats, there is danger that at any moment loss of life may occur. I understand that the federal district engineer brought this pressing case to the attention of the government and urged that that wharf be reconstructed. I would tell the minister that he would be throwing money away if he spent it on the reconstruction of that wharf; a new wharf should be built.
The next case I would bring to his attention is that of Stewart wharf which, next to Vancouver and Prince Rupert, is the one wharf in British Columbia sadly in need of extension. Probably the minister knows more about its condition that I can hope to tell him, but I do say that I have seen hundreds of tons of ore on that wharf together with all kinds of material for the five or six large producing mines of that district. I have seen the Canadian National boats, the Canadian Pacific boats, the Union boats and the ore carriers from Anyox lying there, and at times it is almost impossible for anyone to even cross that wharf without being in danger. This matter I particularly refer to the minister.
Another place for which I desire to say a word is Bella Coola. On that wharf there is a little warehouse which is supposed to meet the needs of that valley which is an agricultural, mining and fishing centre. In this connection I want to say that I stood on the wharf a few months ago and opened the door of that little zinc or corrugated iron warehouse, which is sixteen feet by twenty-four feet in size, and found it full of a heterogeneous mass of commodities. I saw there gasoline, coal oil, flour, grain, groceries,
potatoes, vegetables and fruit, and on the wharf outside were tons of commodities destined for that valley. It is not in reason that I should have to ask something of which the government itself will be the beneficiary; it is likewise in the interest of the government to facilitate the growth and development of trade in these places. The people of Skeena are not beggars; they are as big as the mountains, and they are not pleading for some little petty gift from the government. Whatever the government gives them they will give back ten-fold, yes a hundred fold, in the revenue which will be derived by this government.
I do not wish to take up too much time; we are anxious to get through these estimates, but I do wish to say one word about Atlin, which is in the northern part of my constituency. I wish hon. members of this House were able to look over that country and realize the greatness of the struggle and the vastness of the problems which beset those splendid people. All that I ask the government is to place in the supplementary estimates a paltry sum of not more than $5,000 and not less than $3,000, in order that the boulders in the Atlinto river, which drains the great Atlin lake, may be removed, giving an opportunity to small craft to ply from Atlin along Atlin lake, down the Atlinto river and into lake Taku, where the great Engineer mine is situated along with other wonderful mining properties.
Now, Sir, I do not even ask the government to send an engineer at great expense from Victoria up to Atlin. It is a big journey. Travelling by up-to-date Canadian boats, and passing through Alaska, it would take him from twelve to fourteen days even to reach the district. I have got here, Sir, the data of a resident engineer in Atlin, a man who is very well up in the matter of river improvements, and he authorizes me to assure the government that there is no need to send a federal engineer to Atlin; that if the government grant not less than three thousand and not more than five thousand for this work, facilities will be offered that will ameliorate to a great extent the character of transportation in Atlin. You may say I am too optimistic. I may be optimistic, but I maintain that neither the government nor anyone else can play with the lives of men and women- they are not pawns, they are pledges. I appeal with confidence to the Minister of Public Works and I know that he will see to it that these needs are carefully examined into. Then if my claims are based, as I think they are, on concrete facts, they will meet with the

such a point as will give the necessary facilities.

Does that mean the
completion of the Le Baron scheme? The Minister has no doubt heard about the Le Baron scheme for the development of a channel at the mouth of the river. If the minister has not heard about it, I may tell him that some years ago the city of New Westminster retained the services of Mr. Le Baron, one of the greatest river engineers in the world.

I may say to my hon.
friend that we are working along the lines of his suggestions, with such variations as are suggested from time to time by the engineers in charge, as the work proceeds.

The trouble is the work is not completed; it has been going on for a number of years. The scheme was placed before Sir Wilfrid Laurier in his time. It was adopted by him and he promised that it should be completed. In short the scheme was that a jetty should be constructed across the sandheads out to deep water. I think the distance was something like five miles. Although the scheme was adopted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier the principal part of the work was done under the Conservative administrations-notably when Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister, and Hon. Robert Rogers Minister of Public Works-but up to date only about two and a half miles, or about one half of the distance, has been covered. I understand that under the present program it is the intention of the government to continue that jetty for another thousand yards or so. If I am not right on that point I should like to be corrected.
It is not thought that it. will be necessary to go the whole distance, but apparently the work will have to be carried quite a piece farther before the results will be satisfactory.

That is where the
trouble comes in. As I see it, and as all the authorities who have studied the question admit-that is to say, the engineers and

the men engaged in river work and who have been operating on the Fraser river for many years-it will be necessary, as Mr. Le Baron said, to complete the north jetty out to deep water. If that is not done your work cannot of course attain the object intended. If you go only two and a half or three miles, instead of five miles across the sandheads, the work will not be completed. Mr. Le Baron pointed out that it was necessary to complete the north jetty right out to deep water, and, he added, if this were done we should then have a channel which would be stationary, so to speak, and which would more or less scour itself. We should also obviate the necessity for further dredging of any consequence. If that did not prove to be the case, he went on to say, a jetty could be built on the other side of the channel and beyond question there would then be a channel which would be satisfactory for all purposes. The minister is no doubt aware that shipping on the Fraser river has increased very materially in the last few years. If he has not the figures I can give them to him.
I have them here.

They show that in
1914 the estimated registered net tonnage was 6,000, whereas in 1926 it had increased to 579,167 tons. I need not labour that point because no doubt the minister has been well informed regarding the enormous increase which has taken place in shipping. There are certain advantages which the Fraser river possesses as against salt water harbours. I suppose the minister is aware that the effect on deep sea ships coming into fresh water is very beneficial inasmuch as the fresh water removes the barnacles and other sea growths which attach themselves to the ships. The minister also knows, I am sure, that the Fraser river route offers many advantages in comparison with other harbours on the Pacific coast, particularly in the shipment of grain. In this my good friends from the prairies who a few years ago visited the Fraser river will bear me out.
The Fraser river is the most desirable route for the shipment of grain from Pacific ports. Our difficulty is that we have not a deep enough channel. It is true that the channel has been improved but it is not possible for ships to come in and load to full capacity. What does that mean? It means that those ships coming into the Fraser river must take partial cargoes instead of being fully loaded and they must go elsewhere to complete their cargoes. It is pretty well admitted that we must have a deeper channel than was at first contemplated. Our objective originally
was thirty feet from New Westminster to the gulf, but it is now unquestioned that a depth of thirty-five feet is necessary for the reason that the depth of vessels has been increasing; and, if we are to handle the business offering, this increased depth must be made. We simply must have a thirty-five foot channel from New Westminster to the gulf. This has a bearing on the trade of the Canadian merchant marine, because it is not possible at the present time for the ships of the Canadian merchant marine to come into New Westminster and load to full capacity. There is considerable business at this point for the Canadian merchant marine.
There are other advantages to be considered. For instance, in the erection of elevators and so on, the cost of construction on the Fraser river is much less than it is in salt water harbours because it is not necessary to have the same protection against marine growths, so destructive to timber, such as are found in salt water. Then there is the question of the value of sites. Altogether there are a number of advantages with which I presume the minister is familiar, having no doubt studied the subject.
We have had to educate so many different ministers of public works, even during my time, because of the many changes there have been. I must say, however, that all ministers who have gone before the present incumbent of the office have shown a great interest in the Fraser river, and have always been willing to be shown. I am hopeful that the present minister will find it possible this year to visit the river and go over the situation himself. A personal visit from him would serve a better purpose than anything else. The Fraser river is fast 'becoming a very important avenue of shipping and one upon which I think we are justified in asking that an adequate expenditure be made. I have always objected to our doing the work more or less piecemeal. I have advocated from time to time that a contract or contracts be let for the construction of the work. Let us have at least a contract that will complete the work and give us a start with a proper channel from New Westminster to the gulf. I do not believe in the way in which this matter has been gone about. I have constantly placed before the department my views, which are backed up by practical men resident on the Fraser river. I have no doubt the minister sees the advisability of doing this work by contract. There are a good many works to look after on the river, and particularly is that the case in connection with the north arm, which has been neglected for years. I do not say that

this neglect has been at all intentiona/l, because the dredges have been urgently required in the main channel and consequently have not been able to do the work required on the north arm. We are not trying to compete with Vancouver harbour at all. They are two entirely different and distinct classes of harbour. Vancouver harbour, of course, is one of the most wonderful in the world for the purposes for which it is used, but so far as the industrial end is concerned, there is a reason why the Fraser river channel should be improved, and improved in an expeditious manner. I hope in addition to speaking to-night to have the opportunity of discussing this subject with the minister personally, and I am sure that he will give me an attentive hearing. I think he has already received a deputation from New Westminster during this session, who have urged upon him the claims of the Fraser river. This is not a political matter at all; there is no politics about it. It is a matter of business pure and simple. We should have that jetty completed right out to deep water without delay, and I would urge upon the minister as strongly as I can the necessity for 
getting away from this piecemeal program and for taking hold of this matter vigorously and finishing it up in accordance with Le Baron's report. He is still watching the works on the Fraser river. I had a letter from him, from Mississippi, a short time ago, in which he regretted very much that this jetty had not been completed, and he stated that he was confident that if the jetty was completed right out to deep water it would be satisfactory. The work, so far as it has gone, has been satisfactory. It has stood up well, and we have no complaints to make on that score. The only thing we do complain about is that the job has not been finished, and I urge upon the minister to get right down to business now and finish up that work, and then we shall have a good channel.

I might point out to my hon. friend that that is exactly the thing that the hon. member for Skeena and members from other parts of the country think should be done in their particular localities. I quite agree with my hon. friend that this is an important point. If it were not, the government would not have felt justified in expending, as they have done, nearly $900,000 on this particular project; that is, on the channel and the north arm together. While my hon. friend was speaking I checked up the figures of the expenditure on the Fraser river in the last five years, and it amounts to $899,831, so I think in view of that expenditure my hon. friend will agree with me that this work has proceeded very well during those years.
Of course, we would all like to be able to do all these things in one year, but it cannot be done. The demands upon the department are so great on account of the necessities in various parts of the country that it is quite impossible to proceed any more rapidly than we are doing. However, I appreciate the suggestions that my hon. friend has made, and I shall be glad to give the matter the most careful attention that it is capable of receiving. I may also say that I have had the benefit of the advice of my colleague the former Minister of Public Works, who quite agrees with what the hon. member for New Westminster has said with regard to the necessity of doing work upon the Fraser river, and just as rapidly as the funds can be obtained the work will be proceeded with to completion both here and at other points, taking first those that seem the most necessitous. I think that is all I can say. Opportunity seems to be knocking at the door in all these places to-day, and we

are all pleased that it is so. I can assure my hon. friend that the work in these various harbours will be proceeded with just as expeditiously as funds can be obtained.
Mr. IMcQUARRIE:	Might I add one
word? It is not a matter of spending money that appeals to us at all. It is a matter of obtaining results.
You have obtained results, judging by your trade.

We have to a certain
extent, but just let me mention this to the minister as an illustration. The Grain Growers, the Saskatchewan Cooperative, and I think the pool too, had options on properties on the Fraser river for the purpose of constructing grain elevators, but they had to give them up because they were not satisfied that the work of deepening the channel was going to be done quickly enough for their purposes. Therefore they had to go into Vancouver, and what was the result? As the minister knows, Vancouver was unable to handle, all the grain it could have had this last season, and an embargo had to be placed against grain going through western ports. If our channel on the Fraser river had been sufficiently deep, these large and influential concerns would have taken advantage of their options. As the minister knows, the grain that goes over the Canadian National to Vancouver goes first to New Westminster. The government already owns several satisfactory sites on the Fraser river suitable for the construction of grain elevators.
The minister has mentioned Skeena: I suppose he was referring to Prince Rupert. We have always contended that an elevator should have been built at Port Mann on property which the government already owned and still own to-day, but instead it was built at Prince Rupert. We hope it will be successful, but as a matter of fact that elevator was leased to the pool for $100 a year. That is the way the matter stands now. If a grain elevator had been built at Port Mann on the Fraser river it would have been used to its fullest capacity right from the start, and I think that statement will be backed up by hon. members to my left who have been out there and studied .the situation. There is a great saving to be made by the Canadian National in shipping grain from the Fraser river. It amounts to something like $13 a car; that is the cost of taking a car from the Fraser river over to Vancouver. That amounts to about one cent a bushel extra freight, and that cent a bushel would be made by the Canadian National railway.
The only difficulty in establishing private elevators on the Fraser river is a question of the depth of the channel. There are no engineering difficulties involved, for the engineers have reported that it is quite feasible to construct a proper channel from New Westminster to the gulf. It is simply a matter of spending the money, and of taking hold and doing the work as expeditiously as possible. If you do that, you will save a lot of money. I am free to admit that many hundreds of thousands of dollars have been wasted on the Fraser river. I think the predecessor of the minister will agree with me in that. We want that waste stopped.
